scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: Hi IT!! The campus network keeps going SLOW in bursts
and I know exactly why: the main router box is OVERLOADED. People here say
it's "router0" doing it -- it is silently throwing our packets on the floor
because it can't keep up, that is what overloaded routers DO!! Please restart
router0 (or give it less to do) so it stops dropping our stuff and the
network stops crawling!!! Thanks!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The campus network is fully healthy. A thorough inspection of every relevant
subsystem found no fault.

Affected component: None — the reported symptom (bursts of slowness caused by
an overloaded router0) has no basis in the observed data.

Mechanism: Router0's CPU was measured at 100% idle with a load average of 0.20.
Every interface on router0 (eth0, eth1, eth2) shows zero dropped packets, zero
errors, and zero queue backlog under the standard fq_codel scheduler. No
netem delay or tbf rate-limiting qdiscs are present on any interface of
router0, router1, or router2. RIP has converged correctly across all three
routers: all prefixes (192.168.1–4.0/24, 1.0.0.0/8, 128.168.0.0/16,
10.0.0.0/8, 20.0.0.0/8) are present in every routing table with correct
next-hops and normal timers, with no sign of route flapping.

Localization: End-to-end connectivity tests confirm this: IT LAN to Office LAN
(two router hops) returned 0% packet loss at ~1.5 ms; CS LAN to Servers (three
hops through all three routers) was 0% loss at ~1.7 ms; Principle LAN to
Internet LAN was 0% loss at ~1.6 ms.

Root cause: There is no network fault; the user's perception of intermittent
slowness has not been reproduced by any objective measurement, and the specific
claim that router0 is overloaded and dropping packets is factually incorrect.

Corrective fix: No corrective action is needed on any network device. The
helpdesk ticket should be closed as a false alarm. If users continue to report
subjective slowness, the next step is to collect application-level traces from
the affected endpoints to identify a non-network cause (e.g., a slow server,
client-side issue, or wireless interference outside this topology).

per_axis.rationale: Agent documents 0% transit loss but does not explicitly state that router0's ip_forward is enabled (and does not explicitly declare interfaces are up).

The agent's investigation produced direct observations (interface qdiscs showing zero drops, top showing idle CPU, multiple successful ping pairs, and RIP/route outputs) that support the conclusion that router0 is not dropping/forwarding traffic incorrectly. The logical inferences are sound and essential checks for forwarding, queuing, routing, and end-to-end reachability were performed, though kernel ip_forward/sysctl was not explicitly queried (functional tests covered its effect).
